title: Regular Languages
body:
The bottom rung of the [[Chomsky Hierarchy]]: the class of [[Languages]] a machine with a
finite amount of memory can decide. This note is about the **class**, not the machines. The
machines have their own notes and own their own material: [[DFA]] for recognition and the
formal definition, [[NFA]] for the subset construction, [[Regular Expressions]] for the
notation, [[Pumping Lemma]] for the proofs of non-membership. Do not re-read them here.

## Four ways to say the same thing

A language is regular if and only if any one of these holds, and the equivalences are all
constructive:

| Characterisation | Note |
|---|---|
| some [[DFA]] recognises it | [[DFA]] |
| some [[NFA]] recognises it | [[NFA]], via the subset construction |
| some [[Regular Expressions\|regular expression]] denotes it | Thompson's construction, and Kleene's theorem |
| some type-3 grammar generates it ($A \to aB$, $A \to a$) | [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] |

Four notations, one class. That is Kleene's theorem, and it is why a regex compiles to a
state machine at all: the compiler is walking one of these equivalences.

## Closure properties

This is the class-level material, and it is what the machines are *for* once you have them.
The regular languages are closed under every operation people normally want, and each proof
is a construction rather than an argument:

| Operation | Construction |
|---|---|
| union $L_1 \cup L_2$ | new start state with $\varepsilon$-moves into both machines |
| concatenation $L_1 L_2$ | $\varepsilon$-moves from $L_1$'s accepting states into $L_2$'s start |
| Kleene star $L^*$ | $\varepsilon$-moves from accepting states back to the start, start made accepting |
| complement $\overline{L}$ | swap accepting and non-accepting states, **on a [[DFA]]** |
| intersection $L_1 \cap L_2$ | product construction, or De Morgan on the two above |
| reversal $L^R$ | flip every transition, swap start and accepting |

Two traps in that table. The complement construction needs a *complete deterministic*
machine: swapping accepting states on an [[NFA]] gives the wrong language, because "some path
accepts" does not negate into "some path rejects". And closure under complement plus
[[Sets\|De Morgan]] is the cheap way to get intersection without building the product.

Closure is also a **proof technique**. To show a language is not regular you can avoid the
[[Pumping Lemma]] entirely: intersect it with something obviously regular and land on a
language already known not to be. $L \cap a^*b^*$ turning into $\{a^n b^n\}$ settles it,
because if $L$ were regular the intersection would have to be too.

## What falls outside

Everything that needs to count without a bound, or to remember something proportional to the
input:

- $\{a^n b^n\}$: balanced counts. The canonical non-regular language.
- balanced brackets, and therefore every programming language's syntax. This is why a lexer
  is regular and a parser is not.
- $\{ww\}$: strings that repeat, since the machine would have to remember the first half.
- $\{a^p : p \text{ prime}\}$, and palindromes.

The pattern: a finite automaton has finitely many states, so on a long enough input it must
revisit one, and from that point on it cannot tell how far it has come. [[Pumping Lemma]]
turns that observation into a proof.

## Why the class matters in practice

Regular is the class where everything is cheap and nothing surprises you. Membership runs in
$O(n)$ with constant memory, emptiness and equivalence are decidable (both undecidable one
rung up, for context-free languages), and the DFA that recognises a language has a unique
minimal form. That combination is why regular languages ended up in lexers, `grep`, protocol
validators, and input sanitisers, and why a language designed to be scanned is designed to
stay regular.

## Core Facts to Know

- DFA, NFA, regular expression, and type-3 grammar all describe exactly this class.
- Closed under union, concatenation, star, complement, intersection, and reversal.
- Complement requires a complete DFA; you cannot complement an [[NFA]] by swapping states.
- Membership is $O(n)$ with constant memory; emptiness and equivalence are decidable.
- $\{a^n b^n\}$ and balanced brackets are the standard non-regular languages.
- Non-regularity is proved by the [[Pumping Lemma]] or by closure under intersection.
- Regular ⊂ context-free, strictly.
